content: The study compared the time intervals and outcomes across different models of care for HCV RNA testing and treatment initiation. The findings are as follows: 1. Time from Anti-HCV Testing to RNA Testing: The time between anti-HCV testing and RNA testing was consistent across models of care. The longest pooled times were observed in models 3d (1 day, 95% CI: 1–1, n=762) and 4d (1 day, 95% CI: 0–1, n=1051). In contrast, models 1a, 1b, 2a, 2c, 3b, and 4b had a median time of 0 days (95% CI: 0–0). 2. Time from RNA Testing to Treatment Initiation: The shortest times were observed in models 1a and 2c (0 days, 95% CI: 0–0). Model 2b had a median time of 1 day (95% CI: 1–1, n=33). Model 1d had a median time of 5 days (95% CI: 10–57, n=1610). Model 3b had a pooled median time of 62 days (95% CI: 7–62, n=1984), while model 4b had a median time of 107 days (95% CI: 62–107, n=184), and model 4d had a time of 43 days (95% CI: 31–266, n=712). 3. Point-of-Care (PoC) vs. Lab-Based Assays: PoC assays demonstrated shorter times from RNA testing to results availability compared to lab-based assays. For example, in the study by Saludes et al., the PoC arm had a median time of 1 day (range: 1–8), while the lab-based arm had a median time of 7 days (IQR: 5–11). Similarly, in the Martel-Laferriere study, the time from RNA testing to treatment initiation was shorter in the PoC arm (70 days, IQR: 52–106) compared to the lab-based arm (266 days, IQR: 150–449). 4. Treatment Uptake: The percentage of participants initiating treatment was higher in arms with on-site PoC RNA assays (77%, 95% CI: 72–83, n=23,705) compared to lab-based high-throughput RNA assays (53%, 95% CI: 31–75, n=5820). However, there was variability depending on the model of care and population subgroup. 5. Population Subgroups: Among people who inject drugs and homeless individuals, PoC assays showed higher RNA testing and treatment uptake compared to lab-based assays. For example, model 1 had an RNA testing uptake of 93% (95% CI: 83–99, n=6154), while model 4 had an uptake of 27% (95% CI: 18–38, n=85). For prisoners, PoC assays demonstrated higher treatment uptake compared to lab-based assays, although RNA testing uptake was similar. 6. Cost-Effectiveness: Several studies evaluated the cost-effectiveness of PoC RNA assays. For instance, Mohamed et al. used a Markov model to compare two strategies in a remand prison in England. The simplified strategy, which included PoC RNA testing, was cost-effective with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios ranging from £3565 to £10,300 per QALY gained, well below the national willingness-to-pay threshold of £30,000. The MSF Cambodia study found that a simplified model of care, including PoC RNA testing, was cost-saving compared to a full model of care, with a cost of $91 per QALY gained. 7. Heterogeneity Across Studies: There was considerable heterogeneity in outcomes across studies and models of care. This was influenced by factors such as the location of testing and treatment, the number of visits required, and the use of additional simplification strategies in PoC arms. 8. Limitations: Many comparisons were based on a small number of studies or participants, limiting the ability to draw systematic conclusions. Additionally, some studies were ongoing at the time of analysis, which may have affected the reported outcomes. In summary, PoC RNA assays generally demonstrated shorter turnaround times and higher treatment uptake compared to lab-based assays, particularly in certain population subgroups such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, and prisoners. PoC assays also showed potential cost-effectiveness, although further research is needed to confirm these findings across diverse settings and populations.
